title: Speak to the listener
glance: Shape the answer to who is listening and what they must do with it: value, cost, risk and a recommendation for whoever owns the decision; the how for whoever builds and runs it; a written record when the decision will be questioned later.
story: An architect explains the same design to very different people. A finance chief deciding a budget needs value, cost, risk and a recommendation, in a few minutes. Engineers who will build and run the system need component detail, interfaces and failure handling. A data-protection officer needs data flows and controls. Giving the wrong one of these is a common trap: technically perfect, useless to the listener.

When the listener owns the decision, they still want the architect's view. A balanced list of options with no recommendation pushes the analysis back onto them. The right shape is the real options, their trade-offs in the listener's terms, and a clear recommendation backed by evidence such as eval results.

Some decisions outlive the people who made them. When new managers keep reopening a settled choice, the answer is an architecture decision record (ADR): a short document stating the context, the decision, the options considered and the consequences, kept where the next person will find it.
situation: An architect must explain to a retailer's chief financial officer why the returns assistant should use retrieval over the policy library rather than loading every policy into each request. Both designs pass the eval; retrieval costs less per resolved return. The CFO will approve or reject the budget in a 20-minute meeting next week. What should the architect bring?

options.t: Cost per resolved return for each design, the eval results, the main risk, and a clear recommendation.
A walkthrough of the chunking, embedding and index design, with component diagrams.
An architecture decision record stating the context, the options, the decision and its consequences.
A balanced comparison of both designs with their trade-offs, leaving the choice to the CFO.

worlds.name: As written
worlds.fact: The listener is the CFO, who owns the budget decision and has 20 minutes.
worlds.why: The CFO decides on value, cost and risk. Cost per resolved return, backed by eval numbers, plus a recommendation gives exactly what the decision depends on.

losers.B: Accurate, but chunking and embeddings are not what a budget decision turns on, and they would use up the 20 minutes.
losers.C: An ADR is a record for later readers; it is not the shape of a short pitch to the person deciding today.
losers.D: The CFO owns the decision but expects the architect's view. Options with no recommendation push the analysis back onto the listener.

worlds.name: The listener builds it
worlds.fact: The budget is approved. The listener is now the engineering team who will build the retrieval pipeline and run it on call.
worlds.why: Engineers need the how: components, interfaces, and what happens when something fails. The design walkthrough serves the work they must do.

losers.A: Cost per return and a recommendation answer a decision that has already been made; they do not tell anyone how to build the pipeline.
losers.C: An ADR records why retrieval was chosen; the builders need how it works.
losers.D: The choice is settled. Reopening it as an open comparison wastes the team's time.

worlds.name: The decision keeps coming back
worlds.fact: Retrieval was approved last year. The original team has left, and each new manager asks again why policies are not simply all loaded into every request.
worlds.why: A settled decision that keeps being reopened needs a lasting written record of its context, the options rejected and why, so each newcomer can read it instead of restarting the debate.

losers.A: A fresh pitch answers one manager once; the next newcomer will ask again.
losers.B: Build detail explains how retrieval works, not why loading everything was rejected.
losers.D: Presenting the choice as open invites the same debate again, when the need is to record why it was closed.

signals: “the board decides in a short meeting”
“the team that will build and run it”
“the decision keeps being questioned by new managers”
“present the options” to someone who owns the decision
remember: Ask who is listening and what they must do next. Decision owners get options in their terms plus your recommendation; builders get the how; reviewers get data flows and controls; a decision that keeps returning gets an ADR.

practice.stem: A bank's data-protection officer must sign off a mortgage assistant before launch. She asks the architect what happens to a customer's personal data once they type it into the chat. The sponsor has already approved the budget and the eval results. What should the architect prepare for her?
options: The cost per completed application and the savings expected in the first year.
The eval results, showing answer accuracy across the main question types.
A data-flow diagram: where personal data goes, how long it stays and who sees it.
The prompt templates and tool interface specifications, with their full version history.
practice.why: The deciding fact: the listener is the data-protection officer, and her question is about personal data. Data flows, retention and access controls are what her sign-off depends on.
traps: Works for a sponsor deciding a budget, which is already approved.
Works to show quality, but accuracy does not answer where personal data goes.
Works for engineers changing the system, but it buries the data flow she asked about.

practice.stem: A retailer's chief technology officer will own the on-call rota for a new ordering agent. In a design review she asks what happens when the payment tool times out halfway through an order, because her team must handle these failures at night. What should the architect give her?
options: The business case for the agent: cost per order, the expected savings and the main risks.
The failure path: retry rules, how duplicate payments are prevented, and the alert raised.
A recommendation to approve the agent, with the eval results as the evidence.
Two retry designs with their trade-offs, leaving her team to choose between them.
practice.why: The deciding fact: whatever her title, she asked an operational question for a team that will run the system. Here the technical answer is the right one.
traps: Works for an executive deciding a budget, but she asked how failures are handled.
Works when the listener owns an approval decision; she asked how the system behaves.
Works when the design is still open, but here the team needs the agreed behaviour to run it.

practice.stem: A city council's cabinet must choose between two designs for a residents' enquiry assistant. One resolves 81% of enquiries on the eval; the other costs 40% more and resolves 90%. The cabinet owns the budget decision and has ten minutes for it. What should the architect present?
options: Both designs with cost, resolution rate and risk, and the architect's recommendation.
The recommended design alone, so the cabinet is not distracted by alternatives.
Both designs with cost, resolution rate and risk, leaving the choice fully open.
The technical differences between the designs, including model and retrieval settings.
practice.why: The deciding fact: the cabinet owns a real trade-off between cost and resolution. It needs both options in its own terms and the architect's recommendation.
traps: Works when only one option meets a hard constraint; here both are viable and the cabinet must weigh the trade-off.
Works to show the trade-off, but a decision owner also expects the architect's view.
Works for engineers, but model and retrieval settings are not what the budget turns on.
